record.paper_title: Ductile-to-brittle transition and yielding in soft amorphous materials: perspectives and open questions
record.original_question: How can experiments distinguish wall slip from plasticity localized near the wall, and how much does wall slip contribute to the overall yielding dynamics of colloidal gels and to the differences between yielding under shear and yielding under compression at the particle scale?

evidence.quote: Future work should focus on identifying experimentally the differences and similarities between wall slip and plasticity near the wall, so as to clarify the contribution of wall slip to the overall yielding dynamics, especially in colloidal gels.

This experimental challenge aligns closely with the ones emphasized in Sections 1.1.1 and 1.2.3, i.e., it pertains to understanding the distinct characteristics of the yielding process under shear as opposed to compression, especially at the particle scale.

artifact.category_tag: yielding and wall slip in soft amorphous materials
artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a soft amorphous material (in particular, a colloidal gel composed of attractive Brownian particles forming a percolated network) confined between two solid boundaries and subjected either to simple shear or to uniaxial compression. Near each boundary, two distinct mechanisms can produce a non-affine velocity field relative to the bulk: (i) wall slip, defined as a discontinuity of the tangential velocity at the solid–fluid interface arising from a depletion or lubrication layer with no plastic rearrangement of particles, and (ii) wall-induced plasticity, defined as a thin region adjacent to the wall in which particles undergo irreversible rearrangements (bond breaking/reforming, T1-like events) without an interfacial velocity jump.

Formulate, in a way that can be implemented through rheometric, optical, and particle-tracking measurements at the particle scale, quantitative observables (e.g., local velocity profiles, slip lengths, rates of plastic rearrangements, two-point correlations of particle displacements, stress fluctuations) that unambiguously separate (i) from (ii). Using such observables, determine:

1. The quantitative contribution of wall slip to the overall yielding dynamics of colloidal gels, i.e., how much of the apparent macroscopic yielding strain/stress and of the spatiotemporal organization of plastic events is attributable to interfacial slip versus bulk and near-wall plasticity.

2. The extent to which wall slip accounts for the differences observed between yielding under shear and yielding under uniaxial compression at the particle scale, including any asymmetry in the spatial localization, statistics, and precursors of plastic events between the two loading geometries.

Provide either a theoretical/modeling framework predicting these contributions or an experimental protocol whose outputs determine them.
artifact.status_search_result: The question is posed as an outstanding experimental and conceptual challenge in soft amorphous matter: cleanly distinguishing wall slip from near-wall plasticity, and quantifying slip's role in yielding (especially in colloidal gels) and in the shear-versus-compression asymmetry. Recent literature on yielding of colloidal gels and on wall slip in soft glasses continues to identify this as unresolved, with no consensus quantitative framework available. Status is therefore taken as open.
